members.statement: Default to simplicity: avoid overengineering, simplify scope/design/implementation, and reuse proven solutions before building your own.
Focus on the nature of the solution, not the implementation language: solutions scale, languages do not.
Use the AKF Scale Cube as the framework for scaling: clone (X) for transactions, split different things (Y) by function/resource, split similar things (Z) by customer.
For horizontal read scaling, use master-slave replication (the only approach that scales horizontally): writes at the master, read-only queries on slaves.
Scale out on commodity hardware, not up on big high-end systems, because scaling up follows a power-law cost curve and eventually hits a ceiling.
Own your scalability: scale your own system rather than relying on vendor/proprietary features, keeping destiny, simplicity, and total cost in your control.
Scale out, not up: prefer horizontal scaling by adding more of the same commodity hardware, and reserve vertical scaling for problems with no horizontally-scalable solution.
Account for scaling down as well as up: keep the application able to run on a smaller footprint so falling demand can cut operating cost.
Weigh every scaling decision as a cost-benefit trade-off across capital, complexity, maintenance, and time, remembering the best technical option is not always the right business one.
Use the right storage tool for the data: reserve RDBMS for ACID/relationship needs and choose file systems or NoSQL otherwise, recognizing relationships trade flexibility against scale.
Do not use an RDBMS when ACID is not needed; 'too slow' usually means the wrong tool, so choose data structures and a platform that answer your exact questions cheaply.
Actively use log files — aggregate out-of-band, monitor with automated tools, and assign owners to fix what they reveal — while logging asynchronously to limit cost.
Deliver all logs reliably in real-time over a publish/subscribe substrate with reliable IP multicast, and separate logging roles (publish, journal, analyze) so each scales independently.
Turn the log stream into real-time business-level monitors and build your own cluster tooling from it; correlate technical and business metrics to spot a forming problem.
Cache in depth — CDN, page cache, application cache, object cache — using HTTP headers (not meta tags) and monitoring hit ratios.
The key to caching is understanding your data: how often it changes and where it is used.
Strive for statelessness; if state is required, push it to the browser, and otherwise use a distributed cache without affinity or replication.

Use a collaborative distributed cache so one node's result benefits all and no single failure threatens availability; replicate frequently-read, rarely-changed data to every node since cache replication can be lazy.

Push stable, shared page content out to the web server with two-tier execution so neither the database nor a remote cache is touched, since whole-page transparent caching fails when only part of a page is cacheable.
Treat the message bus as a scalable, fault-isolated component (Y/Z splits, not X) and avoid overcrowding it by publishing only value-justified traffic.
Use a publish-to-a-group messaging bus to decouple clients from servers so a client sends one message and the bus fans it out reliably to all participants.
Treat scalability and performance as distinct properties: a fast component can still fail to scale, and a single slow or non-scaling component can cap or capsize the whole architecture.
Design for scalability from the beginning for the parts that will need it: size for current demand but architect so growth needs no application or architectural redesign.
Build architectures from autonomous, independently scalable components so a demand spike stresses only one or two; component architectures scale better than monoliths.
A service scales when it collects information outside the critical path, so it can run everywhere without loading other components; that, not per-box throughput, is real scalability.
Use version control for everything as the baseline failure-avoidance practice: require atomic commits, run it on every platform you operate, and leverage it for deployment, not just development.
Keep production configuration under version control so non-bare-metal failures are tracked and recoverable; understanding how configuration changed over time beats a point-in-time restore.
Treat high availability and load balancing as orthogonal — HA is resilience to failure, LB is about scale — and define which (or both) a system needs before implementing.
Eliminate single points of failure, including the load balancer itself (deploy two with an HA solution); hardware needed for routine load is not redundant, and selling points are not buying points.

Prefer peer-based high availability — where the cluster owns the services and IP addresses and each node negotiates a subset — over idle hot-standby pairs and dedicated HA hardware as you scale horizontally or across sites.
Base load balancing on effective utilization of available resources, not system load average, which is too stale for short web requests.

Let requirements, not convenience, dictate the load-balancing solution: if a web switch or IPVS cannot meet a functional need it is eliminated, and application-layer balancers buy features (SSL-content and business-rule routing) at a performance cost.
Do not confuse session stickiness with load balancing: pinning a user to a server for locally stored session state creates a single point of failure.
Split session data — frequently used parts in the client's cookie, rarely used parts in a central store — to remove sticky sessions and radically improve load balancing.
Most content is static, so serve it from a lightweight, single-purpose server segregated from dynamic content, allowing each to scale independently.
Align static- and dynamic-content distribution mechanisms to reduce human error, and keep dynamic code consistent across all nodes.
A computer cache is only an optimization — a miss costs only time — so design cacheable data to carry an explicit TTL and treat the cache as purgeable at will.

Choose cache semantics deliberately: TTL caching is easy and approximate, explicit invalidation is complex and correct; for high read-to-write data you control, prefer caching indefinitely and invalidating on change.
Replication is hard because of ACID and you cannot get both availability and performance from multimaster replication; pick the technique that matches the need rather than assuming multimaster.
Survive network partitions in multimaster replication with a quorum algorithm (at most one quorum at any time), tunable to business priorities; EVS gives ordered messaging without 2PC's cost.
